Manichaeism was an ancient Persian religion named after its prophet Mani. At its heart was the belief in two opposing divine powers, one of good and the other of evil. The first was represented by light and the second by darkness. The first created the angels and the world of spirits, while the material world came from the second. Manichaean beliefs played a significant part in Islamic and Christian philosophy in the Middle Ages. See Van Vloten, p. 83. ↩

Ibn al-Rawandi was a Persian from Isfahan who lived in Baghdad. He embraced Mu'tazilite thought, later rejected it and joined the group known as the Rafida, a name used for certain Shia. He wrote a book attacking the Mu'tazilites, The Disgraces of the Mu'tazilites, attributing to them views quite different from their own. Their enemies seized on these statements to attack them and discredit their beliefs. In fact, Ibn al-Rawandi was a heretic who attacked belief in God as Lord and the prophethood of Muhammad; his writings cannot therefore be taken as reliable. The Mu'tazilite al-Khayyat refuted them in his book The Vindication, an answer to the atheist Ibn al-Rawandi. ↩
